subject: Chemistry
scope: Fifteen targeted Chemistry recall reinforcements: 9 AS and 6 already-taught A-level cards; no buffers, NMR or untaught later topics.
notes: Includes user's often-forgotten q=n|ΔH| relationship, signs, calorimetry and Year 2 Kp, Born-Haber and Gibbs. New prompts are independently original but not proof all prior flashcards are exhaustively checked.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: For an exothermic reaction measured using calorimetry, what is the sign of ΔH?
accept: Negative.
ΔH is less than zero.
Enthalpy change is negative.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: In q = mcΔT, what must be done to q if calculated using a temperature rise in °C?
cards.back: The temperature difference can be used directly because a change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K.
accept: The temperature difference can be used directly because a change of 1 °C equals a change of 1 K.
A temperature difference in Celsius has the same numerical size as in kelvin.
No 273 conversion is needed for the temperature change.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What happens to the measured magnitude of an exothermic ΔH when heat escapes to the surroundings?
cards.back: The measured magnitude is smaller than the true value.
accept: The measured magnitude is smaller than the true value.
Heat loss makes the calculated exothermic enthalpy less negative.
The absolute value of ΔH is underestimated.
reject: Heat loss makes the measured ΔH more negative.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What is q when n moles undergo a process with enthalpy change of magnitude |ΔH| per mole?
accept: q = n|ΔH|.
Number of moles multiplied by magnitude of enthalpy per mole.
Energy equals amount times absolute enthalpy change.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When a transition metal atom forms a positive ion, which of its occupied 4s and 3d subshells loses electrons first?
accept: The 4s subshell.
Electrons are removed from 4s before 3d.
The occupied 4s electrons are removed first.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When converting a gas pressure from kPa to Pa, what do you multiply by?
accept: Multiply by one thousand.
Multiply the kPa figure by 10³.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: If doubling one reactant concentration leaves the rate unchanged, what is its order in the rate equation?
cards.back: Zero order with respect to that reactant.
accept: Zero order with respect to that reactant.
The order in that reactant is zero.
Concentration has no effect on rate under those conditions.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What can a positive 2,4-DNPH test establish about an unknown organic substance?
cards.back: It contains an aldehyde or ketone carbonyl group.
accept: It contains an aldehyde or ketone carbonyl group.
The sample may be an aldehyde or a ketone.
The test is consistent with an aldehyde or ketone functional group.
reject: The molecule is definitely an aldehyde.
The molecule must be a carboxylic acid.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: What can distilling off an aldehyde as it forms help prevent when oxidising a primary alcohol?
cards.back: Further oxidation of the aldehyde to a carboxylic acid.
accept: Further oxidation of the aldehyde to a carboxylic acid.
It reduces the chance of the aldehyde being oxidised further.
It removes the aldehyde before further oxidation can occur.
reject: It makes a secondary alcohol into a primary alcohol.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: When using ΔG = ΔH − TΔS, how should ΔS in J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ be handled if ΔH is in kJ mol⁻¹?
cards.back: Convert ΔS to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ by dividing by 1000.
accept: Convert ΔS to kJ K⁻¹ mol⁻¹ by dividing by 1000.
Divide the entropy change in joules by 1000.
Use compatible kilojoule energy units for the entropy term.
reject: Use ΔS in joules without any unit conversion.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Does ΔG below zero guarantee a reaction will proceed quickly?
cards.back: No; the reaction may have a large activation energy.
accept: No; the reaction may have a large activation energy.
No, kinetics and activation energy control how fast it proceeds.
Thermodynamic feasibility does not ensure a fast rate.
reject: Yes, negative ΔG always gives an instant reaction.
Yes, ΔG is the activation energy.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: Why is the second electron affinity normally endothermic?
cards.back: Energy is needed to add an electron to an already negatively charged ion.
accept: Energy is needed to add an electron to an already negatively charged ion.
The incoming electron is repelled by an anion.
Electrostatic repulsion makes the second electron addition require energy.
reject: A second electron is attracted by the negative charge so it releases energy.
It is always equal to the first electron affinity.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: How is the partial pressure of a gas in an equilibrium mixture calculated?
cards.back: Its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure.
accept: Its mole fraction multiplied by the total pressure.
Partial pressure equals mole fraction times total pressure.
p_i = x_i P_total.
reject: Total pressure divided by mole fraction.
Mole fraction divided by total pressure.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: At constant temperature, what happens to the value of Kp if the equilibrium gas pressure is changed?
accept: Kp stays unchanged.
The equilibrium constant remains the same if temperature is fixed.
Kp depends only on temperature for the specified equilibrium.

cards.subject: Chemistry
cards.front: At a temperature where Kw is greater than at 25 °C, can a neutral solution have pH below 7?
cards.back: Yes; neutrality means [H⁺] = [OH⁻], not necessarily pH 7.
accept: Yes; neutrality means [H⁺] = [OH⁻], not necessarily pH 7.
A neutral solution can be below pH 7 at higher temperature.
Equal hydrogen and hydroxide concentrations define neutral even if pH is less than seven.
reject: No, neutrality always means pH exactly 7 at all temperatures.
